title: Variables & Data Types
description: Store values in variables and meet Python's core built-in types.

lesson.title: Variables & Data Types
lesson.summary: Bind names to values and learn the four everyday built-in types.
lesson.body:
## Variables are names for values

In Python you create a **variable** by assigning a value to a name with `=`:

```python
age = 30
name = "Ada"
```

The name on the left now refers to the value on the right. You don't declare a type ahead of time — Python figures it out from the value. This is called *dynamic typing*.

## The everyday built-in types

| Type | Example | Meaning |
|------|---------|---------|
| `int` | `42` | Whole number |
| `float` | `3.14` | Number with a decimal point |
| `str` | `"hello"` | Text |
| `bool` | `True` / `False` | Truth value |

Use the built-in `type()` function to ask Python what type a value is:

```python
type(42)        # <class 'int'>
type(3.14)      # <class 'float'>
type("hello")   # <class 'str'>
type(True)      # <class 'bool'>
```

## Reassigning and re-typing

A variable can be reassigned at any time, even to a value of a different type:

```python
x = 10      # x is an int
x = "ten"   # now x is a str
```

That flexibility is powerful but means you should keep track of what a name holds.

## Converting between types

You can convert values with the type names: `int()`, `float()`, `str()`, `bool()`.

```python
int("5") + 1     # 6  (string "5" becomes the number 5)
str(5) + "!"     # "5!"
float("2.5")     # 2.5
```

This matters because input from a user always arrives as a string — convert it before doing math.

examples.title: Inspect a few values
examples.description: Run it, then change the values and see how the reported types change.
examples.code:
age = 30
pi = 3.14159
name = "Ada"
is_student = True

print(age, type(age))
print(pi, type(pi))
print(name, type(name))
print(is_student, type(is_student))

examples.title: Convert a string to a number
examples.code:
quantity = "5"
print(int(quantity) + 1)   # 6
# print(quantity + 1)      # uncomment to see a TypeError

questions.prompt: Which symbol assigns a value to a variable in Python?
questions.explanation: A single `=` assigns. `==` compares for equality.

questions.prompt: What is the type of the value `3.0`?
questions.explanation: A decimal point makes it a `float`, even though the value equals 3.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
x = 4
x = "four"
print(type(x))
```
questions.explanation: Reassigning `x` to a string makes its type `str`.
`int("7")` converts the string to the number 7, then 7 + 3 = 10.
`True` (no quotes) is a boolean. `"True"` is a string.

flashcards.front: How do you assign a value to a variable?
flashcards.back: With `=`, e.g. `name = "Ada"`. The name on the left refers to the value on the right.

flashcards.front: Name Python's four everyday built-in types.

flashcards.back: Returns the type of the value `x` currently refers to, e.g. `<class 'int'>`.
You don't declare a variable's type; Python infers it from the assigned value, and it can change on reassignment.

flashcards.front: How do you turn the string "5" into the number 5?
flashcards.back: Use `int("5")`. Use `float()` for decimals and `str()` to go back to text.
